blocks.title: Atmosphere and layers
blocks.md: The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases. Layers from the ground: **troposphere** (weather occurs here), **stratosphere** (ozone layer), **mesosphere**, **thermosphere**. In the troposphere temperature falls with height, on average about 6.5°C per 1000 m.

blocks.title: Why latitude matters
blocks.md: Near the equator the Sun’s rays are nearly overhead: they strike a small area and pass through less atmosphere, so heating is intense. Towards the poles the same energy is spread over a larger area and passes through more air. Surfaces with high **albedo** (ice, bright sand) reflect more energy than dark forest.

blocks.caption: Pressure belts and the main surface winds.
blocks.alt: A table of four latitude zones with the usual pressure and wind pattern.

blocks.title: Pressure belts and winds
blocks.md: Heating at the equator makes air rise (low pressure). It sinks near 30° latitude (high pressure, deserts). Winds blow from high to low pressure but are deflected by the **Coriolis effect**: to the right in the northern hemisphere, to the left in the south. This gives the **trade winds** (north-east in the north) and the **westerlies**.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.md:
- Winds are named after where they come FROM: a north-east trade wind comes from the north-east.
- Warm air rises and so gives LOW surface pressure; sinking air gives HIGH pressure.
- Weather occurs in the troposphere, not in the ozone layer.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Temperature and height
blocks.statement: A town at sea level has an average temperature of 28°C. A hill town 1000 m higher is in the same area. Estimate its temperature (use 6.5°C per 1000 m).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Direction of a trade wind
blocks.statement: Explain why the wind at the surface between 30°N and the equator blows from the north-east.
steps: Air moves from the high-pressure belt near 30°N towards the equatorial low, that is from north to south.
The Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the right in the northern hemisphere.
A southward wind deflected to the right becomes a wind from the north-east.
blocks.answer: Pressure gradient plus Coriolis deflection gives the north-east trades.

blocks.title: ITCZ
blocks.md: The **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)** is the belt where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet and air rises, forming thick clouds and heavy rain. It follows the overhead Sun with a delay: it moves north from about March to August and south for the rest of the year.

blocks.title: West African monsoon
blocks.md: When the ITCZ is far north, moist **south-westerly** air from the Atlantic reaches West and Central Africa and brings the rainy season. When it moves south, dry **north-easterly** air from the Sahara dominates: the **harmattan**, a dry, dusty wind in the dry season (roughly November to March).

items.text: Overhead Sun moves north (June to August)
Sun moves south: dry harmattan returns

blocks.caption: How the ITCZ produces seasons.
blocks.alt: A chain of four boxes showing the Sun moving north, the ITCZ moving north, the monsoon rains and the return of the dry harmattan.

blocks.title: Climate types
blocks.md: **Equatorial:** hot all year, small annual temperature range, heavy rain in every month, daily convectional storms. **Tropical continental (savanna):** hot, a longer dry season and one wet season, a larger temperature range. In Cameroon the south has a long, humid, mostly bimodal rain pattern; the north has one rainy season and a long dry season; the Atlantic coast and the slopes of Mount Cameroon are extremely wet.

blocks.title: Do not confuse
blocks.md:
- Rainfall total is not the same as temperature range: range = highest monthly mean − lowest monthly mean.
- The ITCZ is a belt of low pressure and rising air, not a single line fixed on the equator.
- Relief rain on mountains adds to the monsoon effect: windward slopes are much wetter than leeward ones.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Temperature range
blocks.statement: A station’s hottest month averages 31°C and its coolest month 24°C. Another station has 27°C and 26°C. Which is more likely to be equatorial and why?
steps: Equatorial climates have very small ranges, so station 2 is more likely equatorial.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why is Maroua drier than Douala?
blocks.statement: Explain in simple terms why the far north of Cameroon gets less rain than the coast.
steps: The coast is close to the moist Atlantic air and the ITCZ stays near for long.
The far north is far from the ocean and the ITCZ reaches it late and leaves early.
So the northern rainy season is short and the dry harmattan season is long.
blocks.answer: Distance from the moist air source and a short ITCZ stay give the north less rain.

blocks.title: Soil and its profile
blocks.md: **Soil** is a mixture of weathered mineral particles, organic matter, water and air. A **soil profile** has horizons: **O** (litter and humus), **A** (topsoil), **B** (subsoil where leached minerals collect), **C** (weathered parent rock) and **R** (bedrock). Soil forms from parent material, climate, relief, organisms and time.

blocks.title: Tropical soils
blocks.md: In hot, wet forests chemical weathering and heavy rain wash out (**leach**) soluble minerals, leaving iron and aluminium oxides: red, deep, acidic soils (**ferralsols**, often called laterite when hardened). Fertility is low in the soil itself: most nutrients are held in the vegetation and recycled quickly from leaf litter. Clear the forest and the nutrients are soon lost.

blocks.caption: A soil profile from litter to bedrock.
blocks.alt: Five stacked boxes labelled O litter and humus, A topsoil, B subsoil, C weathered rock and R bedrock.

blocks.title: Vegetation
blocks.md: **Tropical rainforest:** tall evergreen trees in layers (emergent, canopy, understorey, floor), buttress roots, drip-tip leaves, high biodiversity. **Savanna:** grassland with scattered fire- and drought-resistant trees such as the baobab, a long dry season, deep roots. **Sahel:** thorny scrub and sparse grass.

blocks.title: Fertile does not mean tropical
blocks.md: Young volcanic soils, such as those around Mount Cameroon and the volcanic highlands of western Cameroon, are generally richer in minerals than old leached soils. Do not say that all tropical soils are infertile.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Why shifting cultivation?
blocks.statement: Explain why farmers using shifting cultivation move to a new plot after a few years.
steps: Clearing and burning releases a short burst of nutrients into the soil.
Crops remove nutrients and heavy rain leaches them.
Yields fall, so the plot is left to fallow and vegetation regrows while the farmer clears elsewhere.
blocks.answer: Nutrients are quickly used and leached, so land is rested.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Adaptation
blocks.statement: Give two adaptations of savanna trees and explain them.
steps: Deep roots reach water during the long dry season.
Some lose leaves in the dry season to cut water loss.
blocks.answer: Thick bark (fire) and deep roots or leaf loss (drought).

exercises.prompt: Describe how the movement of the ITCZ explains the wet and dry seasons in northern Cameroon.
exercises.model: When the overhead Sun and the ITCZ move north, moist south-westerly air spreads over the north, giving the wet season (roughly May to September). When the ITCZ retreats south, dry north-easterly harmattan air returns, giving a long dry season. The wet season is short because the ITCZ is overhead only briefly at that latitude.
